summary: This document defines two COSE header parameters for carrying RFC 3161 timestamp tokens in COSE_Sign and COSE_Sign1 messages. It lets COSE protocols use existing timestamping infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: A timestamp proves something existed by a certain time. This lets signed messages carry such a proof.

questions: cose then timestamp vs timestamp then cose
subtitle: Two COSE header parameters that carry an RFC 3161 timestamp token inside a signed COSE message.

tldr.problem: COSE signed messages have no standard way to carry a trusted timestamp from an RFC 3161 Time Stamping Authority, so signatures cannot easily be shown to predate certificate expiry or key compromise.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9921 defines two header parameters, 3161-ctt (unprotected) and 3161-ttc (protected), each holding a DER-encoded timestamp token as a byte string. They differ in what was hashed and sent to the TSA: the signature in one mode, the payload in the other.
tldr.outcome: Existing RFC 3161 timestamping infrastructure can be used with COSE_Sign and COSE_Sign1. The two modes mean different things, and mixing them up can lead to accepting signatures made after key revocation.

facts.label: Token encoding
facts.value: DER-encoded TST in a CBOR byte string

today: RFC 9921 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2026 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Timestamp COSE Messages
sections.content:
RFC 3161 describes how to timestamp a message digest to prove it was created before a given time. RFC 9921 defines two new CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) header parameters that carry the TimeStampToken (TST) output of that protocol, so that existing and widely deployed trust infrastructure can be used with COSE_Sign and COSE_Sign1 messages. The COSE structures themselves come from RFC 9052.

The RFC gives two use cases. The primary one is long-term signatures: signatures that can still be verified after the signing certificate has expired. A relying party can then be certain the document was signed at least at the time given by the Time Stamping Authority (TSA), and that the certificate was valid when the signature was made.

The second use case is new: notarizing a signed statement by registering it with a transparency service. The log is append-only, so the entry cannot be changed. To avoid losing the TST during registration, it must be included in the signed statement.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you need to prove you signed something before your pen ran out of ink, or before someone lost the key. A trusted clock-keeper's stamp proves it, and this RFC says how to attach that stamp.

sections.title: The Two Modes of Use
sections.content:
There are two ways to combine COSE protection with timestamping. Both are shown in the RFC for COSE_Sign1; COSE_Sign works similarly with several signers and a signatures field in place of signature.

COSE, Then Timestamp (CTT): the signature field of the signed message is hashed and sent to a TSA. The returned token is added back as an unprotected header in the same COSE object. Use it when a record of when the signature operation happened is wanted. The RFC compares such tokens to a countersignature made by the TSA.

Timestamp, Then COSE (TTC): a datum is hashed and timestamped first. The token goes into the protected headers, and the original datum becomes the payload of the COSE Signed Message. This wraps the signed document and its timestamp together in an immutable payload.
sections.plainLanguage: In one mode you sign first and get the stamp afterwards, like stamping a signed letter. In the other you get the stamp first and then sign the letter with the stamp already attached.

sections.title: The 3161-ctt and 3161-ttc Header Parameters
sections.content:
Each mode has its own header parameter, so that their different meanings stay separate. Both contain a DER-encoded TST wrapped in a CBOR byte string (major type 2).

3161-ctt is an unprotected header parameter and MUST be used for CTT mode. The MessageImprint sent to the TSA MUST be the hash of the CBOR-encoded signature field of a COSE_Sign1 message, or of the CBOR-encoded signatures field of a COSE_Sign message. The CBOR encoding includes the byte string heading, such as the bytes 0x5840 in the RFC's SHA-256 example. The hash algorithm SHOULD be the one used for signing, which may not be possible if the token was obtained outside the context where the COSE object is assembled.

3161-ttc is a protected header parameter and MUST be used for TTC mode. The MessageImprint MUST be the hash of the payload of the COSE Signed Message, using only the payload bytes and not the byte string wrapping. Again the signing hash algorithm SHOULD match the one in the MessageImprint, though this may not hold when the timestamp requester and the signer are different entities.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two labelled slots for the stamp. One slot is on the outside of the envelope for the sign-then-stamp case. The other is sealed inside for the stamp-then-sign case. Each slot also says what the clock-keeper was shown.

sections.title: Checking a Timestamp
sections.content:
Timestamp tokens use Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) as their signature envelope, so RFC 5652 covers signature verification and RFC 3161 covers checks specific to timestamp tokens. The signed payload of a token is the TSTInfo structure, which holds the MessageImprint that was sent to the TSA, including the hash algorithm.

As part of signature verification, the receiver MUST make sure the MessageImprint in the embedded token matches a hash of the payload, the signature field or the signatures field, depending on the mode and on the type of COSE structure.

Appendix A of the RFC walks through one TTC and one CTT example. In the TTC example, the payload 'This is the content.' is hashed with SHA-256 and sent to the TSA, and the returned token is placed in the protected headers before signing.
sections.plainLanguage: To check the stamp, you hash the same thing again and see whether it matches what the clock-keeper wrote down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security sections of RFC 3161 and RFC 9052 apply here too, including the need to protect private keys and to report compromised keys promptly. The RFC's threat discussion assumes an attacker can move the clocks of the signer and relying parties but not the TSA, which is a trusted third party. Tampering with the signer's clock then has no effect, since the TSA timestamp becomes the only reliable source of time. Changing the relying party's clock can still cause CMS validation to fail, which is a denial of service.

In CTT mode an attacker could remove or replace the timestamp in the unprotected header, so the signed message should be integrity protected in transit and at rest. In TTC mode the TSA only sees a hash of the payload, but to stop comparison with known payloads the payload would need to be armored, for example with a nonce shared with the recipient but not the TSA. That mechanism is out of scope.

The modes mean different things. Implementers MUST clearly distinguish timestamps proving the payload existed earlier (TTC) from timestamps covering the signature itself (CTT). Confusing them can lead to accepting signatures created after key revocation, so validators should rely only on TSA timestamps that explicitly cover signature data to decide when a signature was made.
sections.plainLanguage: A stamp on the letter only proves the letter existed, not when you signed it. Mixing up the two kinds of stamp would let a cheat sign late and pretend it was early.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has allocated both parameters in the COSE Header Parameters registry. Each has a value type of bstr.

  • 3161-ttc: label 269, described as a timestamp token per RFC 3161, Timestamp, Then COSE (Section 3.2).
  • 3161-ctt: label 270, described as a timestamp token per RFC 3161, COSE, Then Timestamp (Section 3.1).
sections.plainLanguage: Each slot got an official number so everyone uses the same label: 269 for the sealed one and 270 for the outside one.
